---
title: "Eigenvectors — Directions That Do Not Turn"
description: "A compact linear-algebra lesson with mathematical definitions, real values and reasoning."
---

## Start with a question

A transformation stretches one direction three times and another direction twice. Are there arrows whose direction stays unchanged?

## Understand the central idea

An eigenvector is a nonzero direction that a matrix scales without bending it into another direction; its eigenvalue tells how much scaling occurs.

## Express it with mathematics

$$
A\mathbf v=\lambda\mathbf v,\qquad\mathbf v\ne\mathbf0
$$

**Every symbol explained:** A is a square matrix, v is a NONZERO eigenvector, and λ (lambda) is its eigenvalue. The equation says transforming v is equivalent to multiplying it by λ.

**Substitute real numbers:** Take A=[[3,0],[0,2]] and v=(1,0). Av=(3,0)=3v, so λ=3. For v=(0,1), Av=(0,2)=2v, so λ=2. But v=(1,1) becomes (3,2), not a simple multiple of (1,1).

## Why this works

The special directions form solutions of (A−λI)v=0. A nonzero solution exists only when A−λI is singular; in two dimensions this condition becomes a determinant equation.

## What can go wrong?

Some real matrices, such as a 90° planar rotation, have no nonzero REAL eigenvectors, even though complex eigenvalues exist.

## Your turn

For A=[[2,0],[0,5]], find eigenvalues by trying (1,0) and (0,1).
